message.content:
Create realistic Markdown-family documents for testing a Markdown formatter. Write them into /tmp/corpus15/r/ (create it). Do NOT run any formatter or other program on them; just write the files (Write tool or shell heredoc). Do not write anything outside /tmp/corpus15/.

Create 16 files, 60-200 lines each:
1. readme_1.md — README of a popular CLI tool: centered logo HTML block, badges row, "Table of Contents" with nested links, Features list with emoji, Installation (Homebrew, Scoop, cargo, binaries table), Quick start with shell code blocks and output blocks, Configuration with a TOML code block and a table of options (long descriptions), FAQ using `<details>` blocks, Contributors section, License.
2. readme_2.md — README of a Python library: badges, short description, long paragraphs explaining concepts, code examples with `>>>` doctest style, an API overview table, "Comparison with alternatives" table with ✅/❌, citation BibTeX block, acknowledgements.
3. changelog_1.md — Keep a Changelog for a web framework: 10 releases with Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed/Security sections, entries with PR links, code spans, nested sub-bullets, a "Migration notes" paragraph in one release, link references at the bottom.
4. changelog_2.md — a changelog with prose-style release notes: each version heading followed by 1-3 paragraphs of text (long lines), then bullet lists, some "**Breaking:**" bold prefixes, occasional blockquote notes.
5. contributing_1.md — CONTRIBUTING for a monorepo: prerequisites table, setup steps with numbered lists and fenced code, branch naming rules, commit message convention with examples in a code block, PR checklist with task boxes, style guide subsections, release process with nested ordered lists.
6. contributing_2.md — a shorter community-oriented CONTRIBUTING with long paragraphs, a list of ways to contribute, links, a "Good first issues" section, code of conduct reference, and contact info.
7. quarto_report_1.qmd — Quarto HTML report: front matter with `format: html: toc: true, code-fold: true, theme: cosmo`, `execute: echo: false`, Python code cells (`{python}`) with `#| label:`, `#| fig-cap:`, a `::: {.callout-tip}` block, a `::: {.panel-tabset}` with 3 tabs (### headings), inline math and display math with label, a table with caption, footnotes, references section `::: {#refs}`.
8. quarto_report_2.qmd — Quarto presentation-like document (format: revealjs) with slides separated by `##` headings, speaker notes `::: {.notes}`, incremental lists `::: {.incremental}`, columns layout `:::: {.columns}` with `::: {.column width="50%"}`, code with line highlighting `{.r code-line-numbers="2-3"}`, images with attributes.
9. rmarkdown_sentence_wrap_1.Rmd — R Markdown article (front matter with `editor_options:` / `markdown:` / `wrap: sentence`, `bibliography`, `output: html_document: toc: true`), Introduction/Methods/Results/Discussion with multi-sentence paragraphs (some with one sentence per line already, others with long lines), abbreviations (e.g., i.e., et al., Fig., approx., vs.), numbers with decimals, citations [@key; @key2, p. 4], inline R `r round(x, 2)`, R chunks, a bulleted list, footnotes.
10. rmarkdown_sentence_wrap_2.Rmd — a teaching document (front matter as above + `output: learnr::tutorial`) with exercises, chunk options like `exercise=TRUE`, hints, questions in numbered lists, block quotes with tips, sentences ending with ? and !.
11. docs_guide.md — a long documentation page (user guide) with H2/H3 structure, admonition-style blockquotes (`> **Note**`), tables, nested lists, many inline code spans and links, long paragraphs.
12. docs_api.md — API reference page: function signatures in code blocks, parameter tables, definition lists (Term then `: definition`), examples, "See also" lists.
13. adr.md — an Architecture Decision Record: Status/Context/Decision/Consequences sections, bullet pros/cons, long paragraphs, a mermaid code block.
14. security.md — SECURITY.md with supported versions table, reporting instructions, PGP key block in a code fence, timeline list.
15. blog_post.md — a Hugo/Jekyll blog post with YAML front matter (title, date, tags list, categories, draft, description long string), long narrative paragraphs with emphasis, quotes, images, a code block, footnotes.
16. meeting_notes.md — meeting notes with date headings, attendee lists, action items as task lists with @mentions, decisions in bold, nested bullets 3 levels deep, a table of owners.

Make them realistic (real-world tone), with natural imperfections: long lines exceeding 100 characters, inconsistent bullet markers within a document, trailing spaces, occasional double blank lines, mixed emphasis styles. UTF-8, LF line endings. Reply only with the list of files.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

This session has no SendMessage tool, so it cannot message them with it; other sessions can still message this one. To reply, use your host application's own messaging tool if it provides one — otherwise a reply from here is not possible, and if one is needed, tell your user.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

kiln

A fast, cross-platform task runner that reads plain TOML and gets out of your way.
Think make without the tabs, or npm run without the node_modules.

[![CI](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/kiln-cli.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/kiln-cli) [![Homebrew](https://img.shields.io/homebrew/v/kiln)](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/kiln) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/kiln-rs/kiln/total.svg)](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/releases) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%2FApache--2.0-blue.svg)](#license) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1029384756193847296?label=discord&logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/kiln-rs) --- ## Table of Contents - [Features](#features) - [Installation](#installation) - [Homebrew (macOS / Linux)](#homebrew-macos--linux) - [Scoop (Windows)](#scoop-windows) - [Cargo](#cargo) - [Prebuilt binaries](#prebuilt-binaries) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Options](#options) - [FAQ](#faq) - [Contributors](#contributors) - [License](#license) ## Features * ⚡ **Fast.** kiln is a single static binary written in Rust; `kiln --version` returns in under 2 ms on a cold cache. * 📄 **Plain TOML** – no DSL to learn, no significant whitespace, no tabs-vs-spaces holy wars. * 🔗 **Task dependencies** with automatic parallelism: independent tasks run concurrently, up to `--jobs` at a time. * 🧠 *Content-addressed caching* — declare `inputs` and `outputs` and kiln skips tasks whose inputs haven't changed (hashes, not mtimes). - 🪟 __First-class Windows support__. Yes, really: `cmd.exe`, PowerShell and Git Bash are all tested in CI. - 👀 `kiln watch` re-runs tasks when files change, with debouncing and `.gitignore` support - 🐚 Shell completions for bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell and elvish * 🎨 Pretty, _colorized_ output that degrades gracefully when piped (and respects [`NO_COLOR`](https://no-color.org)) ## Installation ### Homebrew (macOS / Linux) ```sh brew install kiln ``` ### Scoop (Windows) ```powershell scoop bucket add extras scoop install extras/kiln ``` ### Cargo If you already have a Rust toolchain (**1.74 or newer**): ```sh cargo install kiln-cli --locked ``` > **Note:** the crate is called `kiln-cli` because `kiln` was already taken on crates.io by an unrelated (and long-abandoned) project. The installed binary is still just `kiln`. ### Prebuilt binaries Grab the archive for your platform from the [latest release](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/releases/latest), unpack it, and drop the `kiln` binary somewhere on your `PATH`. Every archive ships with a `.sha256` checksum next to it. | Platform | Arch | Archive | Notes | |----------|:----:|---------|-------| | Linux | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | statically linked, works on Alpine | | Linux | aarch64 | `kiln-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | Raspberry Pi 4/5, AWS Graviton | | macOS | Apple Silicon | `kiln-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | signed & notarized | | macOS | Intel | `kiln-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | | | Windows | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` | needs the VC++ 2015–2022 redistributable | | FreeBSD | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-freebsd.tar.gz` | community maintained, best effort | ## Quick start Create a `kiln.toml` at the root of your project: ```toml [tasks.build] run = "cargo build --release" [tasks.test] run = "cargo test --all-features" deps = ["build"] ``` Run a task (its dependencies run first): ```console $ kiln test ``` ``` ▸ build cargo build --release Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 0.21s ▸ test cargo test --all-features Running unittests src/lib.rs (target/debug/deps/demo-3f1c2a9b) test result: ok. 42 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out ✔ 2 tasks finished in 3.48s (1 cached) ``` List what's available: ```console $ kiln --list build cargo build --release test cargo test --all-features (deps: build) ``` ## Configuration kiln looks for `kiln.toml` in the current directory and then walks up towards the filesystem root, stopping at the first one it finds (or at a directory containing `.git`). Point it somewhere else with `--file path/to/kiln.toml` or the `KILN_FILE` environment variable. ```toml [settings] shell = "bash" # "sh", "bash", "zsh", "pwsh" or "cmd" jobs = 4 dotenv = [".env", ".env.local"] [tasks.fmt] description = "Format Rust and TypeScript sources" run = ["cargo fmt --all", "npx prettier --write 'web/**/*.{ts,tsx,css}'"] [tasks.web] dir = "web" run = "npm run dev" inputs = ["src/**/*", "package.json"] outputs = ["dist/**"] ``` ### Options | Key | Type | Default | Description | |-----|------|---------|-------------| | `settings.shell` | string | `"sh"` on Unix, `"cmd"` on Windows | The shell used to execute `run` commands. Each command is handed to the shell as a single string, so pipes, redirects, globbing and `&&` behave exactly as they would in your terminal. | | `settings.jobs` | integer | number of logical CPUs | Upper bound on how many tasks may run concurrently. Set it to `1` to force sequential execution, which is handy when debugging an ordering problem or when two tasks fight over the same port. | | `settings.dotenv` | array of strings | `[]` | Files to load environment variables from, in order; later files override earlier ones. Missing files are silently skipped, so it's safe to list `.env.local` even if most people on the team don't have one. | | `settings.color` | string | `"auto"` | Whether to emit ANSI colors. `auto` enables them only when stdout is a TTY and `NO_COLOR` is unset. | | `tasks..run` | string \| array | — (required) | Command(s) to execute. When an array is given the commands run one after another in the same working directory, and the task fails as soon as one of them exits non-zero. | | `tasks..deps` | array of strings | `[]` | Tasks that must finish successfully before this one starts. Cycles are detected at load time and reported with the full path, e.g. `a -> b -> c -> a`. | | `tasks..inputs` / `outputs` | array of globs | `[]` | Used for caching. If none of the files matched by `inputs` changed since the last successful run *and* every `outputs` glob still matches at least one file, the task is skipped and reported as `cached`. | | `tasks..dir` | string | directory of `kiln.toml` | Working directory for the task, relative to the config file. | Every setting can also be overridden from the environment: `KILN_JOBS`, `KILN_SHELL`, `KILN_COLOR`. Set `KILN_LOG=debug` to print the resolved task graph and every cache decision — it's the first thing we'll ask for in a bug report :wink: ## FAQ
How is this different from make? `make` is a build system that people (ab)use as a task runner. It's great at what it was designed for, but `.PHONY` targets, mandatory tabs, and the subtle differences between GNU make, BSD make and whatever ships with Xcode get old fast. kiln only does the task-runner part, and does it the same way on every OS.
Can I use kiln in a monorepo? Yes. Put a `kiln.toml` in each package and add `include = ["packages/*/kiln.toml"]` to the root file. Included tasks are namespaced by directory, e.g. `kiln api:test`.
Why TOML and not YAML? Because `on: yes` should not be a boolean. Also, kiln configs are short enough that YAML's extra features don't pull their weight.
## Contributors kiln wouldn't exist without [everyone who has contributed](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/graphs/contributors). Thank you! 💛 Want to help out? Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and look for issues labelled [`good first issue`](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22). ## License Licensed under either of * Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or ) * MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or ) at your option. Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in kiln by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

[![Tests](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=Q8XK2M1P0Z)](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna)
[![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/aligna/badge/?version=latest)](https://aligna.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest)
[![conda-forge](https://img.shields.io/conda/vn/conda-forge/aligna.svg)](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/aligna)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.8812345.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8812345)

**aligna** is a small, fast library for aligning time series — dynamic time warping (DTW), soft-DTW and a handful of related tools — with a NumPy-first API and optional PyTorch and JAX backends for when you need gradients.

It is used in production for speech keyword spotting, gait analysis and industrial sensor monitoring, and at least once that we know of for comparing the songs of humpback whales. 🐋

## Highlights

* Exact DTW with Sakoe–Chiba and Itakura constraints, arbitrary step patterns and early abandoning
* Soft-DTW and its gradient, on CPU or GPU
- Pairwise distance matrices for *ragged* collections (series of different lengths), parallelised with threads
- DTW barycenter averaging (DBA)
* Zero required dependencies beyond NumPy; Numba, PyTorch and JAX are picked up automatically if installed

## Concepts

Two time series rarely line up exactly. A person saying the same word twice will stretch some syllables and rush others; a machine going through the same duty cycle will idle a little longer one day than the next. Comparing such sequences point by point, with the Euclidean distance say, punishes these harmless shifts in timing just as heavily as genuine differences in shape. **Dynamic time warping** fixes this by finding the cheapest *monotonic* alignment between the two sequences — a path through the matrix of pairwise distances that may repeat elements of either series but never goes backwards in time — and reporting the total cost along that path.

The cost of exact DTW is quadratic in the length of the series, which is fine for a few thousand samples and painful beyond that. In practice you almost always want a _global constraint_: the Sakoe–Chiba band keeps the path within a fixed radius of the diagonal, while the Itakura parallelogram limits its slope. Both make the computation roughly linear in the series length and, as a pleasant side effect, prevent pathological alignments in which a single point of `x` is matched to half of `y`.

Classic DTW takes a hard minimum at every step, so it is not differentiable. *Soft-DTW* (Cuturi & Blondel, 2017) replaces that minimum with a smoothed soft-min controlled by a temperature `gamma`; as `gamma → 0` it recovers ordinary DTW, and for `gamma > 0` it has well-defined gradients everywhere. That makes it usable as a loss function for networks that output sequences, or for computing barycenters ("averages") of a set of series by gradient descent.

aligna implements all three ideas behind the same API, so you can prototype with plain NumPy arrays and switch to `aligna.torch` once you want to backpropagate through the alignment. 

## Installation

```bash
pip install aligna

# with the optional backends
pip install "aligna[torch]"     # PyTorch >= 2.1
pip install "aligna[jax]"       # JAX >= 0.4.20

# or from conda-forge
conda install -c conda-forge aligna
```

aligna requires Python 3.9+ and NumPy 1.23+. If [Numba](https://numba.pydata.org/) is installed it is used automatically, which gives a 10–40× speed-up on the CPU code paths.

## Quick tour

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import aligna
>>> x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> y = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y)
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.path[:5]
[(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]
>>> float(np.linalg.norm(x - y[:6]))  # point-by-point comparison is not zero
2.8284271247461903
```

Adding a global constraint is a single keyword argument:

```python
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y, window=aligna.SakoeChiba(radius=2))
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.normalized_distance   # distance / (len(x) + len(y))
0.0
```

Soft-DTW as a differentiable loss:

```python
>>> import torch
>>> from aligna.torch import soft_dtw
>>> pred = torch.randn(8, 50, 3, requires_grad=True)   # (batch, time, features)
>>> target = torch.randn(8, 64, 3)
>>> loss = soft_dtw(pred, target, gamma=0.1).mean()
>>> loss.backward()
>>> pred.grad.shape
torch.Size([8, 50, 3])
```

Pairwise distances between series of different lengths:

```python
>>> series = [np.sin(np.linspace(0, k, 80 + 10 * k)) for k in range(1, 6)]
>>> D = aligna.cdist(series, metric="dtw", window=aligna.SakoeChiba(10), n_jobs=-1)
>>> D.shape
(5, 5)
>>> bool(np.allclose(D, D.T)) and bool(np.all(np.diag(D) == 0))
True
```


## API overview

| Name | What it does | Backends |
|------|--------------|----------|
| `aligna.dtw(x, y, *, window=None, step="symmetric2", dist="sqeuclidean")` | Exact DTW. Returns a `DTWResult` with `.distance`, `.normalized_distance`, `.path` and, if requested, `.cost_matrix` | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.soft_dtw(x, y, gamma=1.0)` | Smoothed, differentiable DTW | NumPy, PyTorch, JAX |
| `aligna.cdist(X, Y=None, *, metric="dtw", n_jobs=1, **kw)` | Pairwise distance matrix between two collections of (possibly ragged) series | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.barycenter(series, method="dba", max_iter=30)` | DTW Barycenter Averaging, or soft-DTW barycenters with `method="soft"` | NumPy, PyTorch |
| `aligna.SakoeChiba(radius)`, `aligna.Itakura(max_slope)` | Global constraint windows | – |
| `aligna.steps` | Predefined step patterns: `symmetric1`, `symmetric2`, `asymmetric`, `rabinerJuang(...)` | – |
| `aligna.plot.alignment(x, y, path, ax=None)` | Quick matplotlib plot of two series and their warping path | – |

Full reference documentation lives at **[aligna.readthedocs.io](https://aligna.readthedocs.io)**.

## Comparison with alternatives

| | aligna | tslearn | dtaidistance | dtw-python | fastdtw |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Exact DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (approximate) |
| Soft-DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| GPU / autograd | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Multivariate series | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Custom step patterns | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Ragged inputs to `cdist` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Wheels, no compiler needed | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Classification / clustering models | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (clustering only) | ❌ | ❌ |

This table reflects our best understanding as of aligna 0.9 (March 2026). If something is wrong or out of date, please [open an issue](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/issues/new) and we'll fix it. We are genuinely fans of all these projects; in particular, __tslearn__ is a much broader toolkit, and if you want an end-to-end classification pipeline it's probably what you're looking for.

## Citing aligna

If aligna contributes to a publication, please cite it as:

```bibtex
@software{okafor_aligna_2026,
  author    = {Okafor, Chidinma and Lindqvist, Henrik and Mart{\'\i}nez, Paula},
  title     = {aligna: Fast and differentiable time series alignment for {Python}},
  year      = {2026},
  publisher = {Zenodo},
  version   = {v0.9.2},
  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.8812345},
  url       = {https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna}
}
```

If you use soft-DTW, please also cite the original paper:

```bibtex
@inproceedings{cuturi2017soft,
  title     = {Soft-{DTW}: a Differentiable Loss Function for Time-Series},
  author    = {Cuturi, Marco and Blondel, Mathieu},
  booktitle = {Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning},
  series    = {Proceedings of Machine Learning Research},
  volume    = {70},
  pages     = {894--903},
  year      = {2017}
}
```

## Acknowledgements

The soft-DTW kernels started life as a port of Mathieu Blondel's reference [Cython implementation](https://github.com/mblondel/soft-dtw), and the step-pattern machinery borrows heavily, with permission, from Toni Giorgino's [dtw](https://dynamictimewarping.github.io/) package for R and Python. Thanks to the tslearn maintainers for many helpful discussions about API design, and to everyone who has ever filed a bug report with a minimal reproducible example: you are the best.

Development of aligna was partly supported by the Swedish Research Council (grant 2023-04117) and by a NumFOCUS Small Development Grant.

## License

BSD 3-Clause. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# Changelog

All notable changes to Brisk will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]

### Added
- `app.route()` now accepts a `RouteGroup`, so nested routers can share middleware without re-declaring it ([#2291](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2291))

### Fixed
- Streaming responses no longer buffer the first chunk when compression is enabled ([#2302](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2302))

## [4.2.0] - 2026-10-28

### Added
- First-class Web Streams support for request bodies: `ctx.req.body` is a `ReadableStream` when `bodyParser: false` is set ([#2240](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2240))
- New `@brisk/otel` package with OpenTelemetry tracing middleware ([#2251](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2251))
  - Spans are named after the matched route pattern (`GET /users/:id`) rather than the raw URL, to keep cardinality low
  - Honours the standard `OTEL_*` environment variables
  - Propagates W3C `traceparent` headers by default
- `ctx.json()` accepts a `status` option, e.g. `ctx.json(user, { status: 201 })`

### Changed
- The default `maxBodySize` was raised from `1mb` to `4mb` to match common reverse-proxy defaults ([#2238](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2238))
- Route matching is ~18% faster on large route tables thanks to a radix-tree rewrite by @mkowalczyk ([#2219](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2219))

### Deprecated
- `ctx.request` is deprecated in favour of `ctx.req` and will be removed in 5.0. A one-time warning is logged in development.

### Fixed
- Multiple `Set-Cookie` headers were joined with a comma instead of being sent separately ([#2244](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2244))
- Fixed a crash in `serveStatic()` on Windows when the request path contained an encoded backslash (`%5C`)

## [4.1.1] - 2026-09-15

### Fixed
* Type inference for route params broke when a path contained a regex segment like `/:id(\\d+)` ([#2231](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2231))
* `brisk dev` no longer leaks a file watcher on every reload 

### Security
* Upgraded `path-to-regexp` to address a ReDoS with two parameters in a single segment (e.g. `/:a-:b`). Upgrading is **strongly** recommended if you accept user-defined routes.

## [4.1.0] - 2026-08-30

### Added
- `app.onError()` hooks can now be async
- The CORS middleware accepts a function for `origin`: `cors({ origin: (o) => o.endsWith(".example.com") })` ([#2201](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2201))
- Experimental Bun adapter, `@brisk/adapter-bun` — _please_ report issues!

### Changed
- `ctx.redirect()` now defaults to `302` instead of `301`. Permanent redirects are cached aggressively by browsers, which surprised a lot of people ([#2188](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2188))

### Fixed
- `HEAD` requests to routes that only define `GET` now return the correct `Content-Length`

## [4.0.0] - 2026-07-01

This is a major release. The headline changes are that Brisk is now ESM-only and requires Node.js 22 or later.

### Migration notes

Most applications can upgrade by replacing `require("brisk")` with `import { createApp } from "brisk"` and bumping their Node.js version. If you wrote custom middleware against the 3.x `(req, res, next)` signature, wrap it with `fromConnect()` from `@brisk/compat`, which adapts Connect/Express-style middleware to the new `(ctx, next)` model at a small performance cost; we recommend porting hot-path middleware by hand. The `config/` directory convention is gone — pass options to `createApp()` directly or load them with your favourite config library. The [upgrade guide](https://brisk.dev/docs/upgrading/v4) has a full checklist, and `npx @brisk/codemod v4 ./src` automates most of the mechanical changes.

### Added
- `(ctx, next)` middleware signature with full type inference for `ctx.state`
- Built-in request validation via [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev), so it works with Zod, Valibot and ArkType
- `brisk routes` CLI command that prints the route table

### Changed
- **BREAKING:** ESM-only; the CommonJS build has been removed ([#2050](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2050))
- **BREAKING:** the minimum supported Node.js version is now 22.
- **BREAKING:** the `ctx.body` setter is replaced by explicit helpers:
  - `ctx.json()`, `ctx.text()` and `ctx.html()` for buffered responses
  - `ctx.stream()` for streaming
  - `ctx.empty(status)` for `204`/`304`

### Removed
- The `brisk/legacy` entry point
- The `app.listen(port, callback)` overload — use `await app.listen({ port })`
- Support for the `config/` directory convention

## [3.9.2] - 2026-05-19

### Fixed
- Memory leak when a client aborted a request while a `ctx.stream()` was pending ([#2011](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2011))

### Security
- Session cookies now default to `SameSite=Lax` (previously the attribute was not set at all)
- `serveStatic()` rejects paths containing null bytes


## [3.9.1] - 2026-04-02

### Fixed
* Regression in 3.9.0 where trailing slashes were stripped from mounted sub-app paths
    * `/admin/` returned 404 when the sub-app was mounted at `/admin`
    * strict mode (`strictSlash: true`) was not affected

## [3.9.0] - 2026-03-21

### Added
- `ctx.signal`, an `AbortSignal` that fires when the client disconnects
- Per-route `timeout` option

### Deprecated
- The `(req, res, next)` middleware signature. It keeps working in 3.x, but 4.0 will require `@brisk/compat` ([#1974](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/1974))
- `app.listen(port, callback)`

### Fixed
- Query strings with repeated keys (`?tag=a&tag=b`) are now consistently parsed into arrays

## [3.8.0] - 2026-01-12

### Added
- HTTP/2 support behind the `http2: true` option ([#1902](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/1902))
- `ctx.cookies.getAll()`

### Changed
- Development error pages now show the source snippet and a clickable stack trace
  - set `BRISK_ERROR_OVERLAY=0` to turn this off

### Removed
- Support for Node.js 16, which has been end-of-life for well over two years

## [3.7.1] - 2025-11-30

### Fixed
- `ETag` generation for empty bodies
- Typo in the default `X-Content-Type-Options` header (`nosnif` → `nosniff`) 🤦

### Security
- Bumped `cookie` to 0.7.2 to reject out-of-bounds characters in cookie names, paths and domains

## [3.7.0] - 2025-10-08

### Added
- `app.group(prefix, fn)` for grouping routes under a shared prefix
- Typed `ctx.params` for string-literal route paths, e.g. `"/users/:id"` gives `{ id: string }`

### Changed
- The logger middleware emits JSON by default when `NODE_ENV=production`

### Fixed
- `ctx.text()` responses were missing `charset=utf-8` in the `Content-Type` header

[Unreleased]: https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/compare/v4.2.0...HEAD
[4.2.0]: https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/compare/v4.1.1...v4.2.0
[4.1.1]: https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/compare/v4.1.0...v4.1.1
[4.1.0]: https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/compare/v4.0.0...v4.1.0

# Release Notes

Quarry follows [semantic versioning](https://semver.org) for its notebook format and plugin API; the user interface may change in any minor release. Notes for versions before 3.0 are archived on [the website](https://quarry.app/releases/archive).

## Quarry 3.4 — "Basalt" (November 3, 2026)

This release is mostly about speed. We rewrote the result grid from scratch on top of a virtualized canvas renderer, which means scrolling through a million-row result set now feels the same as scrolling through a hundred rows, and memory usage for large results dropped by roughly 70% in our benchmarks. If you've ever watched Quarry freeze for a few seconds after running `SELECT * FROM events` against a production replica (we have, many times), this one's for you.

The other big change is that notebooks can now have *parameters*. Declare a parameter in the notebook settings, reference it in any cell as `{{ start_date }}`, and Quarry renders a small form at the top of the notebook and re-runs dependent cells when a value changes. Parameters are always sent to the database as bind variables, never spliced into the SQL text, so there's no injection risk even when the value comes from a free-text field.

- New result grid with virtual scrolling, column pinning and per-column number formats
- Notebook parameters: text, number, date, date range, and "choice from query"
- `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+E` exports the current result to CSV, Parquet or XLSX without opening a dialog
- ClickHouse driver now supports the native `JSON` column type
- **Breaking:** the `quarry.grid.maxRows` setting has been removed, since the new grid has no hard limit. If you relied on it as a safety net, use the per-connection *row limit* instead.
- Fixed: copying a cell that contains a newline produced invalid TSV on Windows

> **Heads up, plugin authors:** the `ResultView` extension point now receives an Apache Arrow `RecordBatch` instead of an array of row objects. A compatibility shim is in place for 3.4 and 3.5 and will be removed in 3.6.

## Quarry 3.3.2 (September 22, 2026)

A small bug-fix release. The most important fix is for a crash on startup on macOS when the login keychain was locked, which affected people who had "Store passwords in the system keychain" enabled and connected to their Mac over screen sharing. Thanks to everyone who sent crash reports, and especially to Hannes Kröger for bisecting it down to a single commit. 

* Fixed a crash on startup when the macOS keychain is locked
* Fixed autocomplete suggesting columns from the wrong schema when two schemas contain a table with the same name
* The Snowflake driver now honours `CLIENT_SESSION_KEEP_ALIVE`

## Quarry 3.3 (August 12, 2026)

Quarry 3.3 introduces __shared connections__ for teams. An admin defines a connection once — host, port, TLS settings, SSH tunnel, everything except the credentials — and publishes it to the workspace; teammates then add only their own username and password, or sign in with SSO. When the shared definition changes, everyone picks up the update the next time they connect. This has been the most requested feature on the forum two years running, and it turned out to be much harder to get right than we expected, mostly because of the many subtle ways an SSH tunnel configuration can differ between two machines.

We also shipped a long-overdue overhaul of query history. History is now searchable, can be filtered by connection and by outcome (succeeded, failed, cancelled), and records the execution time and row count of every query. It's stored locally and never leaves your machine unless you turn on sync.

- Shared connections (Team and Enterprise plans)
- Searchable, filterable query history
- New `EXPLAIN` visualizer for PostgreSQL and DuckDB, including per-node timings for `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
- **Breaking:** connection files (`.quarryconn`) saved by 3.3 can't be opened by 3.2 or earlier. The first time Quarry migrates a connection file, it keeps a backup of the original next to it.
- Dropped support for macOS 12 Monterey

> Note: this release bundles DuckDB 1.3. Database files created with older DuckDB versions are upgraded in place the first time you open them, so please back up any `.duckdb` files you care about before opening them in 3.3.

## Quarry 3.2.1 (June 30, 2026)

This release fixes a regression in 3.2 where the SQL formatter could move a trailing comment onto the following line, which in the worst case commented out part of a `WHERE` clause. **If you're on 3.2.0 and use "Format on run", please update right away.** We're sorry about this one. The formatter's test suite now includes several hundred real-world queries with comments in awkward places, and "Format on run" is now off by default for new installs, as it always should have been.

- Fixed the formatter moving trailing `--` comments onto the next line
- Fixed "Format on run" being enabled by default


## Quarry 3.2 (June 9, 2026)

The theme of 3.2 is _writing SQL faster_. Autocomplete now understands CTEs, subquery aliases and lateral joins, and ranks suggestions by how often you've used them on the current connection. There's a new built-in formatter (finally!) with a handful of options, and snippets can contain tab stops and placeholders using the same syntax as VS Code.

Under the hood, we moved the editor from CodeMirror 5 to CodeMirror 6. Most people won't notice anything except somewhat better performance on very long queries, but if you have customised keybindings, please double-check them: a few obscure Emacs-style bindings didn't survive the move.

* Context-aware autocomplete for CTEs, aliases and `LATERAL` joins
* Built-in SQL formatter (`Shift+Alt+F`)
* Snippets with tab stops and placeholders
* **Breaking:** custom keybindings that use CodeMirror 5 command names must be updated. Quarry shows a one-time notice listing any bindings it couldn't migrate automatically.
* Vim mode: `:s` substitutions now support the `g` and `c` flags

## Quarry 3.1 (April 2, 2026)

Quarry now runs natively on 64-bit ARM Linux, including the Raspberry Pi 5 and Asahi Linux on Apple Silicon Macs. We also added a portable Windows build that doesn't need administrator rights to install — something several people on locked-down corporate laptops had asked for.

- Linux ARM64 builds (`.deb`, `.rpm` and AppImage)
- Portable Windows build (`.zip`)
- BigQuery: authentication with workload identity federation

> If you installed the 3.1 beta from the AppImage, note that the stable release uses a different app ID.
> Your notebooks are safe, but you'll need to re-pin Quarry to your dock or taskbar.

## Quarry 3.0 (February 17, 2026)

Quarry 3.0 is the first release built on our new plugin architecture, and the first in which every database driver — including the built-in ones — is a plugin. That sounds like an internal detail, and mostly it is, but it means drivers can now be updated independently of the app, and third parties can publish drivers for databases we don't support ourselves. Within a week of the beta there were community drivers for CockroachDB, Trino and, somewhat to our surprise, Firebird.

The notebook format changed too. A 3.0 notebook is a plain Markdown file with fenced SQL code blocks and a small YAML header, so notebooks diff nicely in Git and render reasonably well on GitHub. Notebooks from Quarry 2.x (`.qnb`) are converted automatically when you open them; the original file is left untouched.

Finally, a word of thanks: 3.0 was in public beta for eleven weeks, and more than 1,400 of you sent feedback. A surprising number of the fixes in this release exist because someone took the time to write up exactly what they were doing when things went wrong. Thank you.

- **Breaking:** new notebook format (`.quarry.md`); 2.x notebooks are converted on open
- **Breaking:** the 2.x plugin API is not compatible with 3.0 — see the [migration guide](https://quarry.app/docs/plugins/migrating-to-3)
+ Driver marketplace with signed community drivers
+ Dark mode now follows the OS setting by default

A fast, cross-platform task runner that reads plain TOML and gets out of your way.
Think make without the tabs, or npm run without the node_modules.

[![CI](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/kiln-cli.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/kiln-cli) [![Homebrew](https://img.shields.io/homebrew/v/kiln)](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/kiln) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/kiln-rs/kiln/total.svg)](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/releases) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%2FApache--2.0-blue.svg)](#license) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1029384756193847296?label=discord&logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/kiln-rs) --- ## Table of Contents - [Features](#features) - [Installation](#installation) - [Homebrew (macOS / Linux)](#homebrew-macos--linux) - [Scoop (Windows)](#scoop-windows) - [Cargo](#cargo) - [Prebuilt binaries](#prebuilt-binaries) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Options](#options) - [FAQ](#faq) - [Contributors](#contributors) - [License](#license) ## Features * ⚡ **Fast.** kiln is a single static binary written in Rust; `kiln --version` returns in under 2 ms on a cold cache. * 📄 **Plain TOML** – no DSL to learn, no significant whitespace, no tabs-vs-spaces holy wars. * 🔗 **Task dependencies** with automatic parallelism: independent tasks run concurrently, up to `--jobs` at a time. * 🧠 *Content-addressed caching* — declare `inputs` and `outputs` and kiln skips tasks whose inputs haven't changed (hashes, not mtimes). - 🪟 __First-class Windows support__. Yes, really: `cmd.exe`, PowerShell and Git Bash are all tested in CI. - 👀 `kiln watch` re-runs tasks when files change, with debouncing and `.gitignore` support - 🐚 Shell completions for bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell and elvish * 🎨 Pretty, _colorized_ output that degrades gracefully when piped (and respects [`NO_COLOR`](https://no-color.org)) ## Installation ### Homebrew (macOS / Linux) ```sh brew install kiln ``` ### Scoop (Windows) ```powershell scoop bucket add extras scoop install extras/kiln ``` ### Cargo If you already have a Rust toolchain (**1.74 or newer**): ```sh cargo install kiln-cli --locked ``` > **Note:** the crate is called `kiln-cli` because `kiln` was already taken on crates.io by an unrelated (and long-abandoned) project. The installed binary is still just `kiln`. ### Prebuilt binaries Grab the archive for your platform from the [latest release](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/releases/latest), unpack it, and drop the `kiln` binary somewhere on your `PATH`. Every archive ships with a `.sha256` checksum next to it. | Platform | Arch | Archive | Notes | |----------|:----:|---------|-------| | Linux | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | statically linked, works on Alpine | | Linux | aarch64 | `kiln-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | Raspberry Pi 4/5, AWS Graviton | | macOS | Apple Silicon | `kiln-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | signed & notarized | | macOS | Intel | `kiln-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | | | Windows | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` | needs the VC++ 2015–2022 redistributable | | FreeBSD | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-freebsd.tar.gz` | community maintained, best effort | ## Quick start Create a `kiln.toml` at the root of your project: ```toml [tasks.build] run = "cargo build --release" [tasks.test] run = "cargo test --all-features" deps = ["build"] ``` Run a task (its dependencies run first): ```console $ kiln test ``` ``` ▸ build cargo build --release Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 0.21s ▸ test cargo test --all-features Running unittests src/lib.rs (target/debug/deps/demo-3f1c2a9b) test result: ok. 42 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out ✔ 2 tasks finished in 3.48s (1 cached) ``` List what's available: ```console $ kiln --list build cargo build --release test cargo test --all-features (deps: build) ``` ## Configuration kiln looks for `kiln.toml` in the current directory and then walks up towards the filesystem root, stopping at the first one it finds (or at a directory containing `.git`). Point it somewhere else with `--file path/to/kiln.toml` or the `KILN_FILE` environment variable. ```toml [settings] shell = "bash" # "sh", "bash", "zsh", "pwsh" or "cmd" jobs = 4 dotenv = [".env", ".env.local"] [tasks.fmt] description = "Format Rust and TypeScript sources" run = ["cargo fmt --all", "npx prettier --write 'web/**/*.{ts,tsx,css}'"] [tasks.web] dir = "web" run = "npm run dev" inputs = ["src/**/*", "package.json"] outputs = ["dist/**"] ``` ### Options | Key | Type | Default | Description | |-----|------|---------|-------------| | `settings.shell` | string | `"sh"` on Unix, `"cmd"` on Windows | The shell used to execute `run` commands. Each command is handed to the shell as a single string, so pipes, redirects, globbing and `&&` behave exactly as they would in your terminal. | | `settings.jobs` | integer | number of logical CPUs | Upper bound on how many tasks may run concurrently. Set it to `1` to force sequential execution, which is handy when debugging an ordering problem or when two tasks fight over the same port. | | `settings.dotenv` | array of strings | `[]` | Files to load environment variables from, in order; later files override earlier ones. Missing files are silently skipped, so it's safe to list `.env.local` even if most people on the team don't have one. | | `settings.color` | string | `"auto"` | Whether to emit ANSI colors. `auto` enables them only when stdout is a TTY and `NO_COLOR` is unset. | | `tasks..run` | string \| array | — (required) | Command(s) to execute. When an array is given the commands run one after another in the same working directory, and the task fails as soon as one of them exits non-zero. | | `tasks..deps` | array of strings | `[]` | Tasks that must finish successfully before this one starts. Cycles are detected at load time and reported with the full path, e.g. `a -> b -> c -> a`. | | `tasks..inputs` / `outputs` | array of globs | `[]` | Used for caching. If none of the files matched by `inputs` changed since the last successful run *and* every `outputs` glob still matches at least one file, the task is skipped and reported as `cached`. | | `tasks..dir` | string | directory of `kiln.toml` | Working directory for the task, relative to the config file. | Every setting can also be overridden from the environment: `KILN_JOBS`, `KILN_SHELL`, `KILN_COLOR`. Set `KILN_LOG=debug` to print the resolved task graph and every cache decision — it's the first thing we'll ask for in a bug report :wink: ## FAQ
How is this different from make? `make` is a build system that people (ab)use as a task runner. It's great at what it was designed for, but `.PHONY` targets, mandatory tabs, and the subtle differences between GNU make, BSD make and whatever ships with Xcode get old fast. kiln only does the task-runner part, and does it the same way on every OS.
Can I use kiln in a monorepo? Yes. Put a `kiln.toml` in each package and add `include = ["packages/*/kiln.toml"]` to the root file. Included tasks are namespaced by directory, e.g. `kiln api:test`.
Why TOML and not YAML? Because `on: yes` should not be a boolean. Also, kiln configs are short enough that YAML's extra features don't pull their weight.

# aligna

[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)
[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)
[![Tests](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=Q8XK2M1P0Z)](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna)
[![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/aligna/badge/?version=latest)](https://aligna.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest)
[![conda-forge](https://img.shields.io/conda/vn/conda-forge/aligna.svg)](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/aligna)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.8812345.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8812345)

**aligna** is a small, fast library for aligning time series — dynamic time warping (DTW), soft-DTW and a handful of related tools — with a NumPy-first API and optional PyTorch and JAX backends for when you need gradients.

It is used in production for speech keyword spotting, gait analysis and industrial sensor monitoring, and at least once that we know of for comparing the songs of humpback whales. 🐋

## Highlights

* Exact DTW with Sakoe–Chiba and Itakura constraints, arbitrary step patterns and early abandoning
* Soft-DTW and its gradient, on CPU or GPU
- Pairwise distance matrices for *ragged* collections (series of different lengths), parallelised with threads
- DTW barycenter averaging (DBA)
* Zero required dependencies beyond NumPy; Numba, PyTorch and JAX are picked up automatically if installed

## Concepts

Two time series rarely line up exactly. A person saying the same word twice will stretch some syllables and rush others; a machine going through the same duty cycle will idle a little longer one day than the next. Comparing such sequences point by point, with the Euclidean distance say, punishes these harmless shifts in timing just as heavily as genuine differences in shape. **Dynamic time warping** fixes this by finding the cheapest *monotonic* alignment between the two sequences — a path through the matrix of pairwise distances that may repeat elements of either series but never goes backwards in time — and reporting the total cost along that path.

The cost of exact DTW is quadratic in the length of the series, which is fine for a few thousand samples and painful beyond that. In practice you almost always want a _global constraint_: the Sakoe–Chiba band keeps the path within a fixed radius of the diagonal, while the Itakura parallelogram limits its slope. Both make the computation roughly linear in the series length and, as a pleasant side effect, prevent pathological alignments in which a single point of `x` is matched to half of `y`.

Classic DTW takes a hard minimum at every step, so it is not differentiable. *Soft-DTW* (Cuturi & Blondel, 2017) replaces that minimum with a smoothed soft-min controlled by a temperature `gamma`; as `gamma → 0` it recovers ordinary DTW, and for `gamma > 0` it has well-defined gradients everywhere. That makes it usable as a loss function for networks that output sequences, or for computing barycenters ("averages") of a set of series by gradient descent.

aligna implements all three ideas behind the same API, so you can prototype with plain NumPy arrays and switch to `aligna.torch` once you want to backpropagate through the alignment. 

## Installation

```bash
pip install aligna

# with the optional backends
pip install "aligna[torch]"     # PyTorch >= 2.1
pip install "aligna[jax]"       # JAX >= 0.4.20

# or from conda-forge
conda install -c conda-forge aligna
```

aligna requires Python 3.9+ and NumPy 1.23+. If [Numba](https://numba.pydata.org/) is installed it is used automatically, which gives a 10–40× speed-up on the CPU code paths.

## Quick tour

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import aligna
>>> x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> y = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y)
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.path[:5]
[(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]
>>> float(np.linalg.norm(x - y[:6]))  # point-by-point comparison is not zero
2.8284271247461903
```

Adding a global constraint is a single keyword argument:

```python
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y, window=aligna.SakoeChiba(radius=2))
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.normalized_distance   # distance / (len(x) + len(y))
0.0
```

Soft-DTW as a differentiable loss:

```python
>>> import torch
>>> from aligna.torch import soft_dtw
>>> pred = torch.randn(8, 50, 3, requires_grad=True)   # (batch, time, features)
>>> target = torch.randn(8, 64, 3)
>>> loss = soft_dtw(pred, target, gamma=0.1).mean()
>>> loss.backward()
>>> pred.grad.shape
torch.Size([8, 50, 3])
```

Pairwise distances between series of different lengths:

```python
>>> series = [np.sin(np.linspace(0, k, 80 + 10 * k)) for k in range(1, 6)]
>>> D = aligna.cdist(series, metric="dtw", window=aligna.SakoeChiba(10), n_jobs=-1)
>>> D.shape
(5, 5)
>>> bool(np.allclose(D, D.T)) and bool(np.all(np.diag(D) == 0))
True
```


## API overview

| Name | What it does | Backends |
|------|--------------|----------|
| `aligna.dtw(x, y, *, window=None, step="symmetric2", dist="sqeuclidean")` | Exact DTW. Returns a `DTWResult` with `.distance`, `.normalized_distance`, `.path` and, if requested, `.cost_matrix` | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.soft_dtw(x, y, gamma=1.0)` | Smoothed, differentiable DTW | NumPy, PyTorch, JAX |
| `aligna.cdist(X, Y=None, *, metric="dtw", n_jobs=1, **kw)` | Pairwise distance matrix between two collections of (possibly ragged) series | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.barycenter(series, method="dba", max_iter=30)` | DTW Barycenter Averaging, or soft-DTW barycenters with `method="soft"` | NumPy, PyTorch |
| `aligna.SakoeChiba(radius)`, `aligna.Itakura(max_slope)` | Global constraint windows | – |
| `aligna.steps` | Predefined step patterns: `symmetric1`, `symmetric2`, `asymmetric`, `rabinerJuang(...)` | – |
| `aligna.plot.alignment(x, y, path, ax=None)` | Quick matplotlib plot of two series and their warping path | – |

Full reference documentation lives at **[aligna.readthedocs.io](https://aligna.readthedocs.io)**.

## Comparison with alternatives

| | aligna | tslearn | dtaidistance | dtw-python | fastdtw |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Exact DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (approximate) |
| Soft-DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| GPU / autograd | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Multivariate series | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Custom step patterns | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Ragged inputs to `cdist` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Wheels, no compiler needed | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Classification / clustering models | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (clustering only) | ❌ | ❌ |

This table reflects our best understanding as of aligna 0.9 (March 2026). If something is wrong or out of date, please [open an issue](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/issues/new) and we'll fix it. We are genuinely fans of all these projects; in particular, __tslearn__ is a much broader toolkit, and if you want an end-to-end classification pipeline it's probably what you're looking for.

### Added

### Fixed

## [4.2.0] - 2026-10-28

### Added
- First-class Web Streams support for request bodies: `ctx.req.body` is a `ReadableStream` when `bodyParser: false` is set ([#2240](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2240))

  - Honours the standard `OTEL_*` environment variables

- Route matching is ~18% faster on large route tables thanks to a radix-tree rewrite by @mkowalczyk ([#2219](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2219))

- Fixed a crash in `serveStatic()` on Windows when the request path contained an encoded backslash (`%5C`)

* `brisk dev` no longer leaks a file watcher on every reload 

### Security
* Upgraded `path-to-regexp` to address a ReDoS with two parameters in a single segment (e.g. `/:a-:b`). Upgrading is **strongly** recommended if you accept user-defined routes.

## [4.1.0] - 2026-08-30

### Added
- `app.onError()` hooks can now be async
- The CORS middleware accepts a function for `origin`: `cors({ origin: (o) => o.endsWith(".example.com") })` ([#2201](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2201))
- Experimental Bun adapter, `@brisk/adapter-bun` — _please_ report issues!

## [4.0.0] - 2026-07-01

This is a major release. The headline changes are that Brisk is now ESM-only and requires Node.js 22 or later.

### Migration notes

Most applications can upgrade by replacing `require("brisk")` with `import { createApp } from "brisk"` and bumping their Node.js version. If you wrote custom middleware against the 3.x `(req, res, next)` signature, wrap it with `fromConnect()` from `@brisk/compat`, which adapts Connect/Express-style middleware to the new `(ctx, next)` model at a small performance cost; we recommend porting hot-path middleware by hand. The `config/` directory convention is gone — pass options to `createApp()` directly or load them with your favourite config library. The [upgrade guide](https://brisk.dev/docs/upgrading/v4) has a full checklist, and `npx @brisk/codemod v4 ./src` automates most of the mechanical changes.

### Added
- `(ctx, next)` middleware signature with full type inference for `ctx.state`
- Built-in request validation via [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev), so it works with Zod, Valibot and ArkType
- `brisk routes` CLI command that prints the route table

### Changed
- **BREAKING:** ESM-only; the CommonJS build has been removed ([#2050](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2050))
- **BREAKING:** the minimum supported Node.js version is now 22.
- **BREAKING:** the `ctx.body` setter is replaced by explicit helpers:
  - `ctx.json()`, `ctx.text()` and `ctx.html()` for buffered responses
  - `ctx.stream()` for streaming
  - `ctx.empty(status)` for `204`/`304`

### Removed
- The `brisk/legacy` entry point
- The `app.listen(port, callback)` overload — use `await app.listen({ port })`
- Support for the `config/` directory convention

# Release Notes

Quarry follows [semantic versioning](https://semver.org) for its notebook format and plugin API; the user interface may change in any minor release. Notes for versions before 3.0 are archived on [the website](https://quarry.app/releases/archive).

## Quarry 3.4 — "Basalt" (November 3, 2026)

This release is mostly about speed. We rewrote the result grid from scratch on top of a virtualized canvas renderer, which means scrolling through a million-row result set now feels the same as scrolling through a hundred rows, and memory usage for large results dropped by roughly 70% in our benchmarks. If you've ever watched Quarry freeze for a few seconds after running `SELECT * FROM events` against a production replica (we have, many times), this one's for you.

The other big change is that notebooks can now have *parameters*. Declare a parameter in the notebook settings, reference it in any cell as `{{ start_date }}`, and Quarry renders a small form at the top of the notebook and re-runs dependent cells when a value changes. Parameters are always sent to the database as bind variables, never spliced into the SQL text, so there's no injection risk even when the value comes from a free-text field.

- New result grid with virtual scrolling, column pinning and per-column number formats
- Notebook parameters: text, number, date, date range, and "choice from query"
- `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+E` exports the current result to CSV, Parquet or XLSX without opening a dialog
- ClickHouse driver now supports the native `JSON` column type
- **Breaking:** the `quarry.grid.maxRows` setting has been removed, since the new grid has no hard limit. If you relied on it as a safety net, use the per-connection *row limit* instead.
- Fixed: copying a cell that contains a newline produced invalid TSV on Windows

> **Heads up, plugin authors:** the `ResultView` extension point now receives an Apache Arrow `RecordBatch` instead of an array of row objects. A compatibility shim is in place for 3.4 and 3.5 and will be removed in 3.6.

## Quarry 3.3.2 (September 22, 2026)

A small bug-fix release. The most important fix is for a crash on startup on macOS when the login keychain was locked, which affected people who had "Store passwords in the system keychain" enabled and connected to their Mac over screen sharing. Thanks to everyone who sent crash reports, and especially to Hannes Kröger for bisecting it down to a single commit. 

* Fixed a crash on startup when the macOS keychain is locked
* Fixed autocomplete suggesting columns from the wrong schema when two schemas contain a table with the same name
* The Snowflake driver now honours `CLIENT_SESSION_KEEP_ALIVE`

## Quarry 3.3 (August 12, 2026)

Quarry 3.3 introduces __shared connections__ for teams. An admin defines a connection once — host, port, TLS settings, SSH tunnel, everything except the credentials — and publishes it to the workspace; teammates then add only their own username and password, or sign in with SSO. When the shared definition changes, everyone picks up the update the next time they connect. This has been the most requested feature on the forum two years running, and it turned out to be much harder to get right than we expected, mostly because of the many subtle ways an SSH tunnel configuration can differ between two machines.

We also shipped a long-overdue overhaul of query history. History is now searchable, can be filtered by connection and by outcome (succeeded, failed, cancelled), and records the execution time and row count of every query. It's stored locally and never leaves your machine unless you turn on sync.

- Shared connections (Team and Enterprise plans)
- Searchable, filterable query history
- New `EXPLAIN` visualizer for PostgreSQL and DuckDB, including per-node timings for `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
- **Breaking:** connection files (`.quarryconn`) saved by 3.3 can't be opened by 3.2 or earlier. The first time Quarry migrates a connection file, it keeps a backup of the original next to it.
- Dropped support for macOS 12 Monterey

> Note: this release bundles DuckDB 1.3. Database files created with older DuckDB versions are upgraded in place the first time you open them, so please back up any `.duckdb` files you care about before opening them in 3.3.

## Quarry 3.2.1 (June 30, 2026)

This release fixes a regression in 3.2 where the SQL formatter could move a trailing comment onto the following line, which in the worst case commented out part of a `WHERE` clause. **If you're on 3.2.0 and use "Format on run", please update right away.** We're sorry about this one. The formatter's test suite now includes several hundred real-world queries with comments in awkward places, and "Format on run" is now off by default for new installs, as it always should have been.

- Fixed the formatter moving trailing `--` comments onto the next line
- Fixed "Format on run" being enabled by default


## Quarry 3.2 (June 9, 2026)

The theme of 3.2 is _writing SQL faster_. Autocomplete now understands CTEs, subquery aliases and lateral joins, and ranks suggestions by how often you've used them on the current connection. There's a new built-in formatter (finally!) with a handful of options, and snippets can contain tab stops and placeholders using the same syntax as VS Code.

Under the hood, we moved the editor from CodeMirror 5 to CodeMirror 6. Most people won't notice anything except somewhat better performance on very long queries, but if you have customised keybindings, please double-check them: a few obscure Emacs-style bindings didn't survive the move.

* Context-aware autocomplete for CTEs, aliases and `LATERAL` joins
* Built-in SQL formatter (`Shift+Alt+F`)
* Snippets with tab stops and placeholders
* **Breaking:** custom keybindings that use CodeMirror 5 command names must be updated. Quarry shows a one-time notice listing any bindings it couldn't migrate automatically.
* Vim mode: `:s` substitutions now support the `g` and `c` flags

## Quarry 3.1 (April 2, 2026)

Quarry now runs natively on 64-bit ARM Linux, including the Raspberry Pi 5 and Asahi Linux on Apple Silicon Macs. We also added a portable Windows build that doesn't need administrator rights to install — something several people on locked-down corporate laptops had asked for.

- Linux ARM64 builds (`.deb`, `.rpm` and AppImage)
- Portable Windows build (`.zip`)
- BigQuery: authentication with workload identity federation

> If you installed the 3.1 beta from the AppImage, note that the stable release uses a different app ID.
> Your notebooks are safe, but you'll need to re-pin Quarry to your dock or taskbar.

## Quarry 3.0 (February 17, 2026)

Quarry 3.0 is the first release built on our new plugin architecture, and the first in which every database driver — including the built-in ones — is a plugin. That sounds like an internal detail, and mostly it is, but it means drivers can now be updated independently of the app, and third parties can publish drivers for databases we don't support ourselves. Within a week of the beta there were community drivers for CockroachDB, Trino and, somewhat to our surprise, Firebird.

The notebook format changed too. A 3.0 notebook is a plain Markdown file with fenced SQL code blocks and a small YAML header, so notebooks diff nicely in Git and render reasonably well on GitHub. Notebooks from Quarry 2.x (`.qnb`) are converted automatically when you open them; the original file is left untouched.

Finally, a word of thanks: 3.0 was in public beta for eleven weeks, and more than 1,400 of you sent feedback. A surprising number of the fixes in this release exist because someone took the time to write up exactly what they were doing when things went wrong. Thank you.

- **Breaking:** new notebook format (`.quarry.md`); 2.x notebooks are converted on open
- **Breaking:** the 2.x plugin API is not compatible with 3.0 — see the [migration guide](https://quarry.app/docs/plugins/migrating-to-3)
+ Driver marketplace with signed community drivers
+ Dark mode now follows the OS setting by default
