---
title: "From Makefiles to `{targets}`"
subtitle: "How we made the weekly forecast pipeline reproducible (and a lot faster)"
author: "Lena Hoffmann"
institute: "Data Science Guild"
date: 2026-11-05
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: [default, custom.scss]
    slide-number: c/t
    logo: images/guild-logo.png
    footer: "Data Science Guild · November 2026"
    code-overflow: wrap
    transition: fade
    chalkboard: true
    preview-links: auto
execute:
  echo: true
  eval: false
---

## Where we started

![](images/pipeline-before.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" fig-alt="A tangle of fourteen R scripts connected by arrows, several of them labelled 'run manually'"}

::: {.notes}
Open with the diagram and ask: who has a folder called `final_v2_REAL`? Pause for laughs.

The point is: 14 scripts, run in an order only Marco knew, and Marco is on parental leave until March.
:::

## What hurt

::: {.incremental}
- Re-running *everything* after a one-line change (~3 hours)
- "Works on my machine" — different package versions on every laptop
- No way to tell which outputs were stale 
- The Monday report silently used **last week's** data. Twice.
:::

::: {.notes}
The stale-data incident is what got us the budget for this. Don't dwell on it — the people involved are in the room.
:::

## What `{targets}` gives you

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A declarative pipeline**

- each step is a *target*: a name plus a command
- dependencies are found by static code analysis
- only outdated targets re-run
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
__More or less for free__

* parallel workers via `{crew}`
* targets stored in the cloud (S3, GCS)
* a dependency graph: `tar_visnetwork()`
:::

::::

## A minimal `_targets.R`

```{.r code-line-numbers="2-3"}
library(targets)
tar_option_set(packages = c("dplyr", "readr", "fable"))
tar_source("R/")

list(
  tar_target(raw_file, "data/sales.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(sales, read_sales(raw_file)),
  tar_target(model, fit_models(sales)),
  tar_target(forecast, make_forecast(model, h = "8 weeks"))
)
```

::: {.notes}
Lines 2–3 first: packages, and sourcing our own functions from `R/`.
Then the pipeline itself is just a list. Emphasise `format = "file"` — that's what makes the CSV a tracked dependency, so editing the file triggers a rebuild of everything downstream.
:::

## Running it

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3"}
tar_make()
#> ▶ dispatched target sales
tar_visnetwork(targets_only = TRUE)
```

![](images/visnetwork.png){.r-stretch fig-alt="Dependency graph rendered by tar_visnetwork, with outdated targets highlighted in blue"}

## Making it fast

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.incremental}
- branch over stores with `pattern = map()`
- 8 local workers with `{crew}`
- cache on a shared S3 bucket
:::
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{.r code-line-numbers="2|5-6"}
tar_option_set(
  controller = crew::crew_controller_local(workers = 8)
)
tar_target(
  model, fit_models(sales_by_store),
  pattern = map(sales_by_store)
)
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Dynamic branching: one model per store, 212 stores. With 8 workers the model step goes from ~2 h to ~20 min.
:::

## Results

| | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Full run | 3 h 10 min | 46 min |
| Typical Monday run | 3 h 10 min | **4 min** |
| Stale outputs in report | ¯\\\_(ツ)\_/¯ | 0 |

::: {.notes}
"Typical Monday run" = only the newest week of data changes, so most targets are skipped.
The shrug is deliberate. Wait for the laugh. 
:::


## Lessons learned {.smaller}

1. Write *functions* first. The pipeline is just glue.
2. Keep targets small enough to be cheap to rebuild, but big enough to mean something
3. Use `format = "file"` for anything read from disk
4. Don't put secrets in `_targets.R` — use `.Renviron`
5. `tar_meta()` is your friend when debugging "why did this re-run?"

## Questions? {background-color="#1d3557"}

![](images/qr-repo.png){width="220" fig-align="right" fig-alt="QR code linking to the talk repository"}

Slides and code: <https://github.com/ds-guild/targets-talk>  
Slack: `#guild-reproducibility`

::: {.notes}
If there are no questions, jump to the appendix slide on S3 costs.
:::

## Appendix: S3 costs {visibility="uncounted"}

About **$4.20 per month** for ~38 GB of stored targets, almost all of it forecast objects.

---
title: "Urban heat and pollinator visitation in community gardens"
author:
  - Amara Nwosu
  - Felix Bergström
  - Rosa I. Delgado
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
output:

    toc: true

    number_sections: true

bibliography: references.bib
csl: ecology.csl
link-citations: true
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
  chunk_output_type: console
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(broom.mixed)

visits  <- read_csv("data/visits_2025.csv")
gardens <- read_csv("data/gardens.csv")

n_gardens <- n_distinct(visits$garden_id)
n_obs     <- nrow(visits)
mean_uhi  <- mean(gardens$uhi_intensity, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Introduction

Cities are warmer than the landscapes around them. 
This urban heat island (UHI) effect is typically 1--3 °C on average, but can exceed 7 °C on calm, clear summer nights [@oke1982energetic; @zhao2014strong, p. 217].
Insect pollinators are ectotherms, i.e. their activity depends directly on ambient temperature, so the UHI may change when and how often they visit flowers.

Earlier studies have produced mixed results. Hamblin et al. [-@hamblin2018physiological] found that large-bodied bees declined in abundance along an urban warming gradient in Raleigh, NC, whereas small-bodied taxa were largely unaffected; by contrast, a survey of 12 gardens in Berlin found no detectable effect of local temperature on visitation once floral abundance was accounted for [@vonkonigslow2022; but see @theodorou2020urban]. Most of this work has relied on temperature data from airport weather stations approx. 10--20 km from the study sites, which cannot capture the fine-scale variation that matters to a foraging bee [@hamblin2018physiological; @burdine2019, p. 4].

Here we ask three questions: 

* Does garden-level UHI intensity predict pollinator visitation rates?
* Is the relationship different for bees vs. hoverflies?
* Does the effect depend on the time of day, e.g. is it stronger during the afternoon heat?

# Methods

## Study sites

We surveyed `r n_gardens` community gardens across Greater Manchester, UK, between 1 June and 31 August 2025.
Gardens were chosen to span a gradient of impervious surface cover (12.5--81.0 % within a 500 m buffer) while keeping garden size roughly constant (median 0.21 ha, range 0.08--0.46 ha).
Mean UHI intensity across gardens was `r round(mean_uhi, 2)` °C; see Fig. 1 for the full distribution.

## Temperature measurements

Each garden was fitted with two iButton DS1923 loggers in radiation shields at 1.5 m height, recording every 30 min. Loggers were calibrated against a reference thermometer before and after the field season, and drift was < 0.2 °C in all cases. UHI intensity was defined as the mean difference between garden temperature and a rural reference site at Abbots Moss^[Open heathland approx. 40 km SW of Manchester city centre, at a similar elevation to the study gardens.] between 10:00 and 16:00, i.e. the hours during which surveys took place.

## Pollinator surveys

Visitation was recorded in 10-min timed observations of a standardised 1 m² patch of *Borago officinalis* planted in each garden in April.
Observers recorded every insect that contacted the anthers or stigma and identified it to the lowest practical taxonomic level (usually genus for bees, family for flies).  
Each garden was surveyed on 9 dates, three times per date (morning, midday, afternoon), giving `r n_obs` observation periods in total.

## Statistical analysis

We modelled visit counts with a Poisson generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a log link [@bates2015lme4]. In brief:

- response: number of visits per 10-min observation
- fixed effects: UHI intensity (°C), pollinator group, survey period, and the group × UHI and period × UHI interactions
+ offset: log number of open flowers in the patch
- random intercepts: garden and survey date

All analyses were done in R version `r getRversion()` [@rcore2025].

```{r model, echo=TRUE}
m1 <- glmer(
  visits ~ uhi_intensity * group + uhi_intensity * period + offset(log(n_flowers)) +
    (1 | garden_id) + (1 | survey_date),
  data = visits, family = poisson,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)
coefs <- tidy(m1, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE)
b_uhi <- coefs |> filter(term == "uhi_intensity") |> pull(estimate)
```

# Results

We recorded 4,318 flower visits, of which 61.4 % were by bees (mainly *Bombus* spp. and *Apis mellifera*) and 29.8 % by hoverflies (Syrphidae).
The remaining 8.8 % were by other flies, butterflies and the occasional wasp.

Visitation increased with UHI intensity overall (β = `r round(b_uhi, 2)` per °C), but the effect differed strongly between groups (Fig. 2). For bees, each additional degree of UHI intensity was associated with approx. 14 % more visits per flower (rate ratio 1.14, 95 % CI 1.05--1.24), whereas for hoverflies the estimate was close to zero and slightly negative (RR 0.97, 95 % CI 0.86--1.09). The interaction with survey period was weak. If anything, the positive effect for bees was _smaller_ in the afternoon than in the morning, contrary to our expectation!

```{r fig-visits, fig.cap="Fig. 2: Predicted visits per 100 flowers per 10 min vs. UHI intensity, by pollinator group (midday surveys). Ribbons show 95 % confidence intervals."}
newdat <- expand_grid(
  uhi_intensity = seq(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), max(gardens$uhi_intensity), length.out = 50),
  group = c("bee", "hoverfly"), period = "midday", n_flowers = 100
)
newdat$pred <- predict(m1, newdata = newdat, re.form = NA, type = "response")
ggplot(newdat, aes(uhi_intensity, pred, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "UHI intensity (°C)", y = "Visits per 100 flowers per 10 min", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Discussion

Our results suggest that moderate urban warming may benefit bees in a temperate maritime climate, where cool and cloudy days frequently limit foraging.
This is consistent with the thermal-limitation hypothesis [@kuhsel2015high] and with observations of earlier activity onset in warmer microsites [@fisogni2020; @kammerer2021, pp. 3--5].
Hoverflies, in contrast, did not respond to warming, possibly because many syrphids tolerate low temperatures better than bees do.[^1]

There are several caveats. First, our temperature gradient (`r round(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)`--`r round(max(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)` °C) is modest compared with cities in continental or Mediterranean climates, and the relationship may well reverse above some threshold, e.g. once afternoon temperatures regularly exceed 30 °C. Second, we measured visitation, not pollination effectiveness or bee fitness. Third, 2025 was an unusually warm summer in the UK, which may have compressed the range of conditions we sampled.

Future work should combine fine-scale temperature monitoring with measurements of pollen deposition and pollinator body condition, ideally across several years and cities.


[^1]: Several common UK hoverflies, e.g. *Episyrphus balteatus*, are active at air temperatures as low as 10 °C, whereas most bumblebees must warm their flight muscles to approx. 30 °C before take-off.

# Acknowledgements {.unnumbered}

We thank the 23 garden groups who hosted loggers and borage patches, and the volunteers who spent approx. 300 hours watching flowers.
Funded by NERC grant NE/X012345/1.

---
title: "Data wrangling with dplyr: filter, arrange and summarise"
author: "Intro to R for Life Scientists — Week 3"
output:
  learnr::tutorial:
    progressive: true
    allow_skip: true
    df_print: paged
runtime: shiny_prerendered
description: >
  Learn to subset rows, sort data and compute grouped summaries with dplyr,
  using the Palmer penguins data set.
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
library(gradethis)
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
tutorial_options(exercise.timelimit = 60, exercise.checker = gradethis::grade_learnr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
```

## Welcome

Welcome to week 3! In this tutorial you'll learn three of the most useful verbs in dplyr: `filter()`, `arrange()` and `summarise()`. 
By the end you should be able to answer questions like "which island has the heaviest penguins?" with just a few lines of code.

We'll use the `penguins` data from the **palmerpenguins** package, which contains measurements of 344 penguins from three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.
Have a look at the first few rows:  

```{r peek, echo=TRUE}
head(penguins)
```

> **Tip:** you can run the code in any exercise box as many times as you like. Nothing you do here can break _anything_, so experiment!

## Filtering rows

`filter()` keeps the rows that match a condition. For example, this keeps only the Adelie penguins:

```{r filter-demo, echo=TRUE}
penguins |> filter(species == "Adelie")
```

Notice the double equals sign `==`. A single `=` is used for naming arguments, not for testing equality, and mixing them up is the single most common error in this tutorial!

### Exercise 1

Filter `penguins` to keep only the birds from **Biscoe** island.

```{r filter-island, exercise=TRUE}
penguins |>
  filter(___)
```

```{r filter-island-hint-1}
penguins |>
  filter(island == ___)
```

```{r filter-island-hint-2}
# Remember that text values need quotes
penguins |>
  filter(island == "Biscoe")
```

```{r filter-island-check}
grade_this_code()
```

### Exercise 2

Now combine two conditions. Keep the penguins that live on Dream island *and* weigh more than 4000 g.
What happens if you use `|` instead of `,` between the conditions?

```{r filter-two, exercise=TRUE, exercise.lines=5}

```

```{r filter-two-solution}
penguins |>
  filter(island == "Dream", body_mass_g > 4000)
```

> 💡 **Did you know?** Comparisons with `NA` return `NA`, and `filter()` silently drops those rows.
> Try `filter(penguins, sex != "male")` and count the rows. Is it what you expected?

## Sorting with arrange()

`arrange()` reorders rows. Wrap a column in `desc()` to sort it in descending order.

```{r arrange-ex, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE}
penguins |>
  arrange(desc(bill_length_mm))
```

Questions to think about: 

1. Which species has the longest bill in the data set?
2. Where do the `NA` values end up when you sort: at the top or at the bottom? Does `desc()` change that?
3. Can you sort by two columns at once? Try `arrange(island, body_mass_g)`.

## Grouped summaries

The real power of dplyr comes from combining `group_by()` with `summarise()`.
The code below computes the mean body mass of each species.
Why do we need `na.rm = TRUE`?

```{r summarise-ex, exercise=TRUE}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r summarise-ex-hint}
# Try removing na.rm = TRUE and see what happens!
```

### Exercise 3

Modify the code above to also compute the number of penguins in each group (`n()`) and the maximum flipper length. Then sort the result so that the heaviest species comes first.

```{r summarise-full, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="summarise-ex"}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    ___
  )
```

```{r summarise-full-solution}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    max_flipper = max(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_mass))
```

## Quiz

```{r quiz}
quiz(
  question("Which function keeps the rows that meet a condition?",
    answer("select()"),
    answer("filter()", correct = TRUE),
    answer("arrange()"),
    answer("mutate()"),
    allow_retry = TRUE
  ),
  question("What does `arrange(desc(x))` do?",
    answer("Sorts by x from smallest to largest"),
    answer("Sorts by x from largest to smallest", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Removes the column x"),
    random_answer_order = TRUE
  )
)
```


## Wrapping up

Well done, you made it! You now know how to subset, sort and summarise a data frame.
In this tutorial you practised:

- `filter()` to keep the rows that match one or more conditions
- `arrange()` and `desc()` to sort rows
* `group_by()` together with `summarise()` to compute one summary per group
* `n()` to count rows inside `summarise()`
